slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/6
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: ng/mL, µg/L

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/6
bullets: What it is used for: Ferritin is often ordered as part of a group of iron tests.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/6
bullets: It helps diagnose or rule out hemochromatosis (iron overload), iron deficiency anemia, liver diseases (much of the body’s ferritin is stored in the liver), restless legs syndrome and adult Still disease; monitor chronic conditions that affect iron (cancer, kidney disease, autoimmune diseases); find low iron before symptoms in people at high risk (being underweight, heavy menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, poor absorption such as with inflammatory bowel disease or after gastrointestinal surgery); and check how well treatment is working.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 4/6
bullets: Serum ferritin is currently the most efficient and cost-effective test for diagnosing iron deficiency. Because it falls during the first stage of iron depletion, it can identify low iron status before anemia develops.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 5/6
bullets: Ordered with symptoms of low iron (shortness of breath, weakness, dizziness, arrhythmia, pale skin, restless legs syndrome) or high iron (weakness, joint pain, loss of interest in sex, abdominal pain, gray, metallic or bronze skin), and when other blood tests show low hematocrit or hemoglobin.
Physiology: Ferritin is a protein that binds to iron and stores it in the body. A ferritin test shows how much iron is stored in the body.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 6/6
bullets: Nearly all ferritin is inside cells; a small amount circulates in the plasma. Under normal conditions serum ferritin is directly related to the amount of stored iron: 1 µg/L of serum ferritin is equivalent to about 10 mg of stored iron.

slides.title: Ferritin

rows: Women who test positive for anemia by hemoglobin or hematocrit — Older (1998) guidance: > 15 µg/L suggests iron deficiency is not the cause of the anemia. Newer sources use a different cut-off (see above).

slides.title: Ferritin

rows: Apparently healthy adults and children aged 5 and over (pregnancy: first trimester) — Under 5 years the cut-off is <12 µg/L.
Adults and children aged 5 and over with infection or inflammation — Under 5 years the cut-off is <30 µg/L. Conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: Higher than normal ferritin can be caused by too much iron in the body. Other causes include inflammation (for example, from infection or surgery), an autoimmune disorder, liver disease, cancer, obesity, alcohol use disorder and hyperthyroidism.
High: A high ferritin level is typical in people who have hemochromatosis. Ferritin tests are also used to see whether iron levels are improving with treatment.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: Lower than normal ferritin may mean iron deficiency anemia or another condition related to low iron. Without treatment, iron deficiency anemia can lead to heart problems, infections, and slow growth and brain development in children.

Low: Iron deficiency develops in stages: 1) storage iron depletion — serum ferritin and bone marrow iron decrease; 2) iron-deficient erythropoiesis — stores are depleted and transferrin saturation declines, but hemoglobin is usually normal; 3) iron deficiency anemia — hemoglobin and hematocrit fall and red cells are small with little hemoglobin (microcytic, hypochromic anemia).

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask you to fast for 12 hours before the test, which is usually done in the morning.

Interferences: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: chronic infection, inflammation or diseases that damage tissues and organs (hepatitis, cirrhosis, neoplasia, arthritis) can raise it independent of iron status. This rise can mask depleted iron stores.
Certain medicines can decrease or increase ferritin levels; an abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: WHO (2020) recommends assessing ferritin together with two acute-phase proteins, CRP and AGP, where infection or inflammation is widespread; with inflammation the iron-deficiency cut-off is raised (adults <70 µg/L, children under 5 <30 µg/L).

Limitations: Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation) can be difficult to diagnose: although low serum ferritin indicates iron deficiency, ferritin tends to be higher with infection or inflammation. In this anemia, inflammatory cytokines raise hepcidin and iron is diverted from the circulation to storage sites.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: In the anaemia algorithm ferritin is the first test in microcytic (low MCV) anaemia: a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; with normal or high ferritin, anaemia of chronic disease (inflammation), thalassaemia and other causes are considered. Full path: Learn → Tables and algorithms → Anaemia.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/4
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: µg/dL, µmol/L

What it is used for: Types of iron tests: serum iron (the amount of iron in the blood), transferrin (the protein that moves iron through the body), TIBC — total iron-binding capacity (how well iron attaches to transferrin and other blood proteins) and ferritin (how much iron is stored). Sometimes one test is ordered, sometimes several to understand the results better.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/4
bullets: Iron tests are most often used to check whether iron is too low (a sign of anemia, although not everyone with low iron has anemia); diagnose different types of anemia; check whether iron is too high (hemochromatosis, or iron overload, which can be inherited or caused by another condition); measure iron stored in the liver to check for liver disease; check for restless legs syndrome and adult Still disease; and see whether treatment for low or high iron is working.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/4
bullets: Symptoms of low iron include weakness or fatigue, dizziness, shortness of breath and arrhythmia. Symptoms of high iron include weakness or fatigue, joint pain (most often in the knees or hands), abdominal pain, loss of interest in sex or erectile dysfunction, and skin that looks gray, metallic or bronze. Low iron may not cause symptoms until it is very low, so a routine test may be ordered.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 4/4
bullets: Physiology: Iron is a mineral the body needs for growth and development. It is used to make hemoglobin, the red blood cell protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body. Iron is also important for healthy muscles, bone marrow and organ function, and for making some hormones. It comes from food or supplements.

Most of the 3 to 4 g of iron in adults is in hemoglobin. Much of the rest is stored as ferritin or hemosiderin in the liver, spleen and bone marrow, or is in muscle myoglobin. Transferrin is the main blood protein that binds and transports iron. The hormone hepcidin is the key regulator of iron absorption and distribution.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: If one or more iron tests show high iron, it may mean hemochromatosis, lead poisoning or liver disease.

Low: If one or more iron tests show low iron, it may mean iron deficiency anemia (a common type of anemia), another type of anemia, or thalassemia (an inherited blood disorder in which the body makes fewer healthy red blood cells).

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: Conditions that raise the risk of iron-deficiency anemia include blood loss (gastrointestinal bleeding from inflammatory bowel disease, an ulcer, colon cancer or celiac disease; injury or surgery; heavy periods or bleeding in childbirth; regular aspirin or NSAID use; urinary tract bleeding); problems absorbing iron (celiac disease, ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s disease, Helicobacter pylori infection, stomach or intestinal surgery, endurance sports); kidney disease; and long-lasting inflammatory conditions such as congestive heart failure or obesity.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask you to fast for 12 hours before the test, which is usually done in the morning. The amount of iron in the blood varies through the day and may be higher in the morning.

Interferences: Many factors affect serum iron: it rises after each meal, infections and inflammation can lower it, and diurnal variation makes it rise in the morning and fall at night. Its day-to-day variation within a person is greater than that of hemoglobin and hematocrit.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Some medicines, including birth control pills and estrogen treatments, can affect iron levels, and iron may be lower in women during their menstrual cycles. So an abnormal result does not necessarily mean a condition that needs treatment.

Limitations: To understand the result, the provider considers symptoms, age, medical history and other blood tests. Hemoglobin, hematocrit, a complete blood count and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) may also be ordered to check iron levels.

slides.title: Serum iron (Fe)
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Each test assesses a different aspect of iron metabolism, so the results of one test may not always agree with another. Lack of standardisation among the tests limits comparison of results between laboratories.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: µg/dL, µmol/L, g/L, %
What it is used for: When hemochromatosis is suspected, doctors may check levels of iron and transferrin, the ratio of iron to transferrin, and ferritin.

Physiology: Transferrin is the protein that moves iron throughout the body; a transferrin test measures it. TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) measures how well iron attaches to transferrin and other proteins in the blood.
TIBC reflects the availability of iron-binding sites on transferrin: it increases when serum iron (and stored iron) is low and decreases when they are high.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Transferrin saturation shows the extent to which transferrin has vacant iron-binding sites (low saturation means a high proportion of vacant sites). It is calculated from two measurements: transferrin saturation (%) = serum iron (µg/dL) / TIBC (µg/dL) × 100. Saturation is highest in newborns, decreases by age 4 months, and then increases through childhood and adolescence to adult levels.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Reference values and decision limits

rows: Transferrin saturation: used to confirm iron deficiency

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Reference values and decision limits
rows: Transferrin saturation: used to confirm iron deficiency
Adults — CDC (1998). Among non-pregnant women of childbearing age, sensitivity 20% and specificity 93% (against absent stainable bone-marrow iron).

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: A high ratio of iron to transferrin (transferrin saturation) may suggest hemochromatosis. The CDC report (1998) describes transferrin saturation as the recommended screening test for hemochromatosis: a repeated high value indicates hemochromatosis.

A transferrin saturation of less than 16% among adults is often used to confirm iron deficiency. Saturation indicates iron-deficient erythropoiesis rather than iron depletion, so it is less sensitive to changes in iron stores than serum ferritin.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: In iron-deficient erythropoiesis (marginal, mild functional deficiency), iron stores are depleted and transferrin saturation declines, but hemoglobin is usually still within the normal range.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask you to fast for 12 hours before the test, which is usually done in the morning.

Interferences: Inflammation, chronic infection, malignancies, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome and malnutrition can lower TIBC, while oral contraceptives and pregnancy can raise it. Even so, its day-to-day variation is less than that of serum iron.

Factors that affect serum iron and TIBC — iron status, diurnal variation and day-to-day variation — also affect transferrin saturation; its diurnal variation is larger than that of hemoglobin or hematocrit.

slides.title: Transferrin, TIBC and transferrin saturation
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: TIBC is less sensitive to iron deficiency than serum ferritin, because changes in TIBC occur only after iron stores are depleted.

Read iron tests together: in iron deficiency serum iron and transferrin saturation are low, TIBC is usually high and ferritin is low; in anaemia of inflammation (chronic disease) iron and TIBC are low while ferritin may be normal or high. Dolgov et al. cite the soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR), which changes little with inflammation, to tell the two apart.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: g/L, g/dL

What it is used for: A hemoglobin test is most often used to check for anemia, a condition in which the body does not make enough healthy red blood cells. Hemoglobin is usually measured as part of a complete blood count (CBC).

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: The test may be part of a routine exam or ordered for symptoms of anemia (weakness, dizziness, cold hands and feet); a family history of thalassemia, sickle cell anemia or another inherited blood disorder; a diet low in iron and other minerals; a long-term infection; or heavy blood loss from an injury or surgery. It is also used to monitor treatment of anemia and other conditions that affect hemoglobin.

Physiology: Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein in red blood cells. It carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body; cells need oxygen to grow, reproduce and make energy. Hemoglobin levels give information about the health of red blood cells.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: High hemoglobin may be a sign of lung disease, heart disease, polycythemia vera (the bone marrow makes too many red blood cells) or sleep apnea (breathing repeatedly stops during sleep). Living at a higher altitude can also raise hemoglobin.

Low hemoglobin may be a sign of different types of anemia, thalassemia, iron deficiency, liver disease, cancer and other diseases, blood loss from injury, a heavy menstrual period or other problems, or a lack of nutrients such as iron or vitamin B12.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: WHO (2024) also grades anemia severity by hemoglobin. In adults aged 15–65, mild anemia is 110–119 g/L in non-pregnant women and 110–129 g/L in men; moderate is 80–109 g/L; severe is below 80 g/L. In all trimesters of pregnancy, severe anemia is below 70 g/L.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/9
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a hemoglobin test. If other tests are ordered on the same sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/9
bullets: WHO recommends measuring hemoglobin in venous blood on automated hematology analyzers with high-quality control measures. Capillary and venous results clearly differ, but the size of the difference has not been confirmed, so no adjustment is given to make capillary results comparable with venous ones.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/9
bullets: Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/9
bullets: Interferences: Diet, activity level, certain medicines, dehydration, smoking and certain genetic conditions can affect the result.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/9
bullets: WHO recommends adjusting for the elevation of residence above sea level and for smoking when diagnosing anemia: the adjustment is subtracted from the observed hemoglobin or added to the anemia cutoff. For example, the adjustment is 8 g/L for 1000–1499 m and 5 g/L for smoking 10–19 cigarettes a day.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 6/9
bullets: On analysers haemoglobin can be falsely high with lipaemia, marked leukocytosis or paraproteinaemia, which make the lysate turbid. If haemoglobin does not fit the RBC and MCV, the result is checked.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 7/9
bullets: Limitations: The test cannot tell what causes an abnormal level, but how high or low it is helps judge severity. The reference range varies with the laboratory, age, race and sex; results are interpreted with symptoms, history and other blood tests.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 8/9
bullets: The WHO cutoffs are based on the 5th percentile of healthy people: about 5% of healthy individuals have hemoglobin below the cutoff and may be falsely diagnosed as anemic.
A hemoglobin test is not the same as a hemoglobin A1C test, which checks average blood glucose.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 9/9
bullets: The Sahli (acid haematin, visual comparison) method is obsolete: the WHO manual calls the haemiglobincyanide photometric method the most accurate and recommends it wherever possible. Aripova et al. (2007) also note that Sahli is not standardised.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: fL

What it is used for: MCV is usually part of a complete blood count. Because each type of anemia affects red cell size, shape and quality differently, MCV helps identify the type of anemia together with other tests.
Physiology: MCV measures the average size of red blood cells. Cells that are too small or too large may be a sign of anemia, a lack of certain vitamins or other conditions.
NHLBI reports MCV in femtoliters (fL); a femtoliter is a measure of volume.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: Larger-than-normal red cells may be a sign of pernicious anemia (from a lack of vitamin B12 or a disease that affects its use, such as certain autoimmune diseases, celiac disease or Crohn’s disease), anemia from a lack of folic acid, or liver disease.

Red cells that are smaller than normal may be a sign of certain anemias, including iron deficiency anemia (the most common form), or of thalassemia (a group of inherited disorders with fewer healthy red cells and less hemoglobin, which can cause severe anemia).

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Interferences: Age, diet, activity level, medicines, menstrual period and other conditions can affect MCV; an abnormal value does not always need treatment.

MCV can be falsely high with cold agglutinins, hyperglycaemia and prolonged sample storage (red cells swell; Dolgov et al. cite storage longer than 8 hours). Severe hyponatraemia can falsely lower it. A sudden change that does not fit previous results suggests an error.
Limitations: MCV alone cannot diagnose a disease. Anemia can occur with a normal MCV — for example, after sudden blood loss, in kidney failure or in aplastic anemia.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Read MCV together with RDW: low MCV with normal RDW — uniform microcytosis (thalassaemia trait, some anaemia of chronic disease); low MCV with high RDW — iron deficiency likely (check ferritin and transferrin saturation); normal MCV with high RDW — mixed populations (early iron deficiency, combined iron + B12/folate deficiency, after transfusion). The reticulocyte count separates poor production from loss or destruction.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous or fingertip capillary blood; heel stick in babies

What it is used for: For a blood smear, blood is spread on a glass slide and treated with a special stain; a laboratory professional then checks the size, shape and number of red cells, white cells and platelets under a microscope. Automatic computer programs may be used to help.

A blood smear alone can't diagnose a disease, but with other tests it helps diagnose and monitor blood and bone marrow disorders, certain cancers of the blood, bone marrow and lymphatic system, infections and certain parasites.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: After an abnormal CBC, a smear confirms cell size and number and shows more about how the cells look, including their color. It is also ordered for symptoms of a blood-cell condition (fatigue, jaundice, unusual bleeding, easy bruising, fever, bone pain, swollen lymph nodes), to check treatment of anemia or blood cancer, and for flu-like symptoms in people living in or travelling to areas where malaria or babesiosis is common.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Results describe what the cells look like and how many there are, and anything else unusual, such as parasites. Abnormal red cells may be a sign of anemia, sickle cell disease, hemolytic anemia, thalassemia or bone marrow disorders; abnormal white cells of infection, leukemia or bone marrow disorders; abnormal platelets of thrombocytopenia, thrombocytosis or thrombocythemia.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, though fasting may be required if other tests are ordered. Blood is drawn from a vein, sometimes by finger prick, and from the heel in babies.
Interferences: Severe illness, stress and blood transfusions can also cause abnormal smear results.
Limitations: Smear results alone usually can't diagnose a condition: the provider combines them with history, symptoms and other tests and may order more tests to find the cause.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Overview
bullets: Diagnosis uses a complete blood count, hemoglobin, blood iron and ferritin; in iron-deficiency anemia iron and ferritin are low. The cause is also sought: gastrointestinal bleeding, heavy periods, surgery, aspirin/NSAID use and others.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Tests to consider · 1/2
rows: Complete blood count: hemoglobin, red cells, hematocrit, MCV
Red cell count, hemoglobin, hematocrit or MCV outside the normal range may signal anemia.
Shows how much iron is stored in the body; low in iron-deficiency anemia.
The amount of iron in the blood; low in iron-deficiency anemia.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Tests to consider · 2/2
rows: The iron-carrying protein (transferrin) and how well iron attaches to it (TIBC).
Finding the cause: stool blood testing, colonoscopy or endoscopy help find a source of bleeding.
Monitoring whether treatment works; oral iron often takes 3–6 months to restore iron levels.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Result patterns
rows: Iron-deficiency anemia is likely; the cause (blood loss and others) is sought.
Possible iron-deficiency anemia, another type of anemia, or thalassemia.
Ferritin <15 µg/L (healthy adults) or <70 µg/L (with inflammation)
Iron deficiency per WHO (2020); CRP (and AGP) are measured to assess inflammation.
Heterogeneous microcytosis typical of iron deficiency; confirm with ferritin and transferrin saturation.

slides.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Cautions
bullets: Birth control pills and estrogen affect iron levels; levels may be lower during menstruation. Iron is higher in the morning — the test is usually done in the morning after a 12-hour fast.

slides.title: 1. Is there anaemia?
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Defined by haemoglobin. WHO (2024): <120 g/L in non-pregnant women aged 15–65, <130 g/L in men; cut-offs are adjusted for age, pregnancy, altitude and smoking.
First check that the result is genuine — see “Analyser spurious results”.

slides.title: 2. Type by MCV
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Low MCV (≈ <80 fL): Microcytic: mostly iron deficiency; thalassaemia → ferritin, iron studies
Normal MCV: Normocytic: acute blood loss, kidney disease, chronic disease, aplastic anaemia → reticulocytes decide
High MCV (≈ >100 fL): Macrocytic: B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease, alcohol, hypothyroidism → B12, folate

slides.title: 3. Marrow response — reticulocytes
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: High (≈ >80×10⁹/L): Bleeding, haemolysis or recovery after treatment → haemolysis markers
Low (≈ <20×10⁹/L with severe anaemia): Poor production: deficiencies, kidney, marrow disease
Cut-offs are approximate; use the absolute count or a corrected index (CRC, RPI) rather than the percentage.

slides.title: MCV with RDW
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: MCV ↓, RDW normal: Thalassaemia trait, some anaemia of chronic disease
MCV ↓, RDW ↑: Iron deficiency (ferritin, transferrin saturation)
MCV normal, RDW ↑: Early iron deficiency, mixed deficiency, after transfusion
MCV ↑, RDW ↑: B12 or folate deficiency, myelodysplasia

slides.title: Iron: deficiency or inflammation?
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Iron deficiency: Ferritin ↓, iron ↓, transferrin saturation ↓, TIBC usually ↑
Anaemia of inflammation: Iron ↓, TIBC ↓, ferritin normal or ↑
Ferritin cut-off (WHO 2020): Healthy adults <15 µg/L; with inflammation <70 µg/L (with CRP, AGP)

slides.title: Haemolysis markers
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Reticulocytes ↑, LDH ↑, indirect bilirubin ↑, haptoglobin ↓.
The Coombs (antiglobulin) test identifies immune haemolysis; spherocytes suggest a membrane defect, schistocytes thrombotic microangiopathy.
A marked LDH rise with haemosiderinuria — intravascular haemolysis.

slides.eyebrow: Microscopy atlas · 1/2
slides.caption: White blood cell at the centre (neutrophil): white cells are typically seen in a peripheral blood smear. Neutrophils are a type of white cell and one of the body's main defences against infection; finding them in a smear is normal. Numerous red blood cells: they carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and return carbon dioxide to the lungs.

slides.caption: Many red cells in a smear are normal; a high number may be linked to polycythaemia or dehydration. Platelets (dot-like bodies): small cell fragments involved in clotting and wound healing, seen as small dots. A normal platelet number is essential for clotting; low counts (thrombocytopenia) or abnormal function can cause bleeding disorders.

healthy women >150, men >200; unwell adults >500 µg/L
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

slides.title: A patient with an active infection has a normal ferritin. Does this prove iron stores are adequate?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: No, inflammation can raise ferritin and mask low stores
Yes, a normal ferritin always proves stores are adequate
Yes, because infection only lowers ferritin
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. That is why ferritin is interpreted with other markers during inflammation.

Basis: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: inflammation raises it regardless of iron status and can mask depleted stores.

slides.title: Serum iron is 9.0 µmol/L (50 µg/dL) and TIBC is 71.6 µmol/L (400 µg/dL). What is the transferrin saturation?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is below the 16% cut-off used in adults to confirm iron deficiency.

Basis: Transferrin saturation (%) = serum iron / TIBC × 100 = 50 / 400 × 100 = 12.5%.

slides.title: According to WHO (2024), below which hemoglobin level is a non-pregnant woman aged 15–65 considered anemic?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the cutoff for non-pregnant women aged 15–65 is 120 g/L (12.0 g/dL).

Basis: WHO Table 2: non-pregnant women < 120 g/L (12.0 g/dL), men < 130 g/L (13.0 g/dL), first and third trimesters < 110 g/L (11.0 g/dL).

slides.title: A patient lives 1,200 m above sea level. What does WHO recommend when assessing anemia?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: An adjustment — 8 g/L (0.8 g/dL) — is added to the cutoff
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: or it is subtracted from the observed value — same result.

Basis: The altitude adjustment — 8 g/L (0.8 g/dL) for 1000–1499 m — is subtracted from observed hemoglobin or added to the anemia cutoff.

slides.title: MCV is low (small red cells). Which causes does the source give?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Small cells: iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia. Large: B12/folate deficiency, liver disease.

slides.title: MCV is normal. Does that rule out anemia?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Yes, a normal MCV rules it out
No, e.g. after sudden blood loss
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Anemia can occur with a normal MCV: sudden blood loss, kidney failure, aplastic anemia.

slides.title: Anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common anemia; causes: chronic blood loss (menorrhagia in women, GI bleeding), increased demand (pregnancy, growth), malabsorption (celiac disease, gastrectomy, H. pylori), inadequate dietary intake.
2. Stages: first the stores are depleted (ferritin↓), then iron delivery is impaired (TSAT↓, CHr↓), and finally Hb falls – Hb is a late sign.

3. Laboratory criteria: ferritin <30 ng/mL or TSAT <20% – absolute iron deficiency (StatPearls); AGA/ASH recommend ferritin <45 ng/mL for IDA; WHO 2020: <15 µg/L in healthy adults, <70 µg/L in infection/inflammation; serum iron varies through the day and is unreliable alone.

slides.title: Anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Blood: microcytic hypochromic anemia, RDW↑, anisopoikilocytosis, "pencil" cells, target cells; reticulocytes low/normal; thrombocytosis may occur.
5. Differentiation: thalassemia trait (ferritin normal, RDW often normal, Hb electrophoresis), anemia of chronic disease (ferritin normal/high), sideroblastic anemia.
6. Response to treatment: 1–2 weeks after iron is given, reticulocytes rise, then Hb; looking for the cause (source of bleeding) is mandatory.

slides.title: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Peripheral blood: Hb decreased, MCV <80 fL, MCH and MCHC low (hypochromia), RDW increased; the smear shows microcytes, anisopoikilocytosis, elliptocytes ("pencil" cells), target cells.
2. Reticulocytes normal or low (absolute count low), CHr/Ret-He <28 pg; platelets often normal or reactively increased.

3. Bone marrow (rarely needed for diagnosis): erythroid hyperplasia, predominance of small early erythroid cells with "ragged" cytoplasm; with Perls stain (Prussian blue) there is no iron in macrophages and sideroblasts are sharply reduced.

slides.title: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Bone marrow iron is the gold standard for assessing stores, but invasive; in practice replaced by ferritin and TSAT.
5. Differentiation: in anemia of chronic disease, iron in bone marrow macrophages is preserved/increased; in sideroblastic anemia – ring sideroblasts.

slides.title: Iron metabolism. The role of transferrin, ferritin, hepcidin?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Iron absorption in the duodenum: dietary Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ and enters the enterocyte; basolateral exit via ferroportin, then it is oxidized and binds to transferrin.
2. Transferrin carries iron in the blood and delivers it to cells via transferrin receptors; TIBC is the total iron-binding capacity of transferrin, TSAT = serum iron/TIBC.
3. Ferritin is the intracellular iron storage protein; serum ferritin reflects stores (low – deficiency), but as an acute-phase protein it rises in inflammation.

slides.title: Iron metabolism. The role of transferrin, ferritin, hepcidin?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Hepcidin is a liver hormone that degrades ferroportin: with iron excess and in inflammation (IL-6) it rises, reducing absorption and release from macrophages; in deficiency and hypoxia it falls.
5. Clinical reflection: iron deficiency (ferritin↓, TSAT↓, transferrin↑), anemia of inflammation (ferritin normal/↑, TSAT↓, hepcidin↑), iron overload/hemochromatosis (TSAT and ferritin↑).
